title: Cursor pagination that survives new rows
prompt:
Teachers in the reading app scroll a feed of reading sessions, newest first. Sessions keep arriving while they scroll. The starter uses offset pagination (the cursor is just an encoded offset), and it already passes some tests. Run them to see which ones it fails and why.

Rewrite listPage(rows, { limit, cursor }) to use keyset (cursor) pagination:

  • rows is the whole table: an array of { id, createdAt, ... } in any order. createdAt is an ISO string (they compare correctly as strings); id is a string.
  • Order: createdAt descending, then id descending as a tie-breaker, so the order is total.
  • Return { items, nextCursor }. nextCursor is an opaque string the client sends back to get the next page, or null when there are no more rows.
  • The cursor must point at the last item returned (its createdAt and id), not at a position. New rows inserted at the top must not shift later pages.
  • limit defaults to 20 and is clamped to 1..100.
  • A garbage cursor throws an Error whose message includes invalid cursor (your API would turn that into a 400).
const p1 = listPage(rows, { limit: 3 });
// p1.items: the 3 newest sessions, p1.nextCursor: "WyIyMDI2LTA5..." (opaque)
const p2 = listPage(rows, { limit: 3, cursor: p1.nextCursor });
// p2.items: the next 3, even if new sessions were added in between

btoa/atob and JSON are available for encoding the cursor.

tests.name: first page: newest 3 and a string cursor
walking every page returns each row exactly once, then null
no extra empty page when the count divides evenly
new sessions arriving between pages cause no duplicates
ties on createdAt are broken by id (descending)
limit defaults to 20 and is clamped to 1..100
a garbage cursor throws 'invalid cursor'

hints: Watch the failing test about new sessions. Page 1 was s010, s009, s008. Two newer rows arrive, so offset 3 now points at s010 again. The fix: remember which row you stopped at, not how many rows you skipped.

Put the last item's createdAt and id in the cursor, e.g. btoa(JSON.stringify([last.createdAt, last.id])). On the next call, decode it and keep only rows that sort after that pair in your order. To know whether there is another page, take limit + 1 rows and check if you got the extra one.

One comparison function does both the sort and the filter:

function compare(a, b) {
  if (a.createdAt !== b.createdAt) return a.createdAt < b.createdAt ? 1 : -1;
  if (a.id !== b.id) return a.id < b.id ? 1 : -1;
  return 0;
}
// rows after the cursor: sorted.filter(r => compare(r, after) > 0)

Wrap the decode in try/catch and check the shape, then throw new Error('invalid cursor').
explain:
This is exactly how the Slack, Stripe and GitHub list APIs page: an opaque cursor that encodes the sort key of the last row. In SQL it becomes WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 21, and with an index on (created_at, id) the database jumps straight to the right spot, so page 500 costs the same as page 1. With OFFSET 10000 the database still walks and throws away 10,000 rows.

The cursor is opaque on purpose: clients can't build or edit it, so you can change what's inside later (add a filter, switch the sort key) without breaking anyone.

Say it: "For an infinite-scroll feed I'd use cursor pagination keyed on (created_at, id). It stays correct while new rows arrive and every page is an index seek. The cost is no jump-to-page-N, which a feed doesn't need. For an admin table where people do want page numbers, offset is fine at small sizes."
